name: William Ewart Gladstone
summary: Gladstone was a free-trader and fiscal economiser who moved from High Church Toryism to leading the Liberal Party. He extended the franchise, disestablished the Irish Church, legislated on Irish land and sought Home Rule for Ireland within the Empire, while defending constitutional monarchy, the family and the limits of women's public role. In foreign affairs he stressed the Concert of Europe, the equal rights of nations, arbitration and restraint in armaments and annexation.

free-trade.rationale: In the Midlothian speeches he calls protection a mischievous and impoverishing system, defends the free-trade work of a generation and argues from the growth of exports since it was adopted.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: He opposed proposals to revert to protection and attacked 'reciprocity' as a quack remedy, and he counted the tariff reforms of 1842-60 first among his own achievements.

free-trade-promotes-peace.rationale: Morley reports that the 1860 commercial treaty with France was meant, in Gladstone's and Cobden's hope, to produce a lasting 'pacification of feeling' between the two countries.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: He denounced the Conservative government's accumulated deficits and praised the surpluses left by his own finance, treating deficits as a mark of bad management.

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: His budgets remitted duties on tea and other common articles and he planned in 1873 to abolish the sugar duties, though he judged indirect taxes would persist.

abolish-income-tax.rationale: He proposed in 1853 that the income tax end after seven years and planned its abolition in 1873, yet in office he kept it, raising and lowering the rate for years.

property-fundamental.rationale: The 1881 Land Act set up courts to fix fair rents and gave Irish tenants fixity of tenure, overriding landlords' freedom to deal with their holdings as they liked.

property-franchise.rationale: He argued in 1864 that any man not presumably disqualified by personal unfitness or political danger is morally entitled to the vote, and the household franchise of 1884 is among the measures he listed as his own.

gradual-change.rationale: In the 1864 franchise speech he kept his protest against sudden, violent, excessive or intoxicating change while arguing for admitting fit working men.

separate-church-state.rationale: He disestablished the Irish Church in 1869 on the ground that its truth-based claim to establishment had been abandoned, but held that an established church is justified where the legislature believes its doctrine true.

national-church-status.rationale: His own account says an establishment is defensible only while the state holds its doctrine to be true; he acted to end the Irish establishment while that principle was still his stated ground for others.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: On the 1870 Education Act he cared for the 'integrity of religious instruction'; he preferred letting local boards prescribe religious teaching and would accept secular state teaching only if religion could be taught in the school at other times.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: He fought the 1857 Divorce bill, calling divorce with the right to remarry an immense evil, and resisted even its fault-based provisions.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: In 1870 he urged the cabinet to speak with the neutral Powers against the transfer of Alsace and Lorraine without reference to the populations, saying transfer by force calls for the reprobation of Europe.

disputed-territory-plebiscite.rationale: His 1870 cabinet memorandum argued that the wishes of the population should govern the fate of Alsace and Lorraine, a principle he also saw as important for the eventual Eastern settlement.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: He told Midlothian audiences that the sanctity of life in an Afghan hill village is as inviolable before God as their own, and that mutual love is not limited by national shores.

arbitrator-settles-disputes.rationale: His government submitted the Alabama claims to arbitration at Geneva and paid the award, which Morley calls a signal victory of preventive diplomacy.

arms-reduction.rationale: In 1894 he opposed the cabinet's naval increases as 'militarism', writing that he had uniformly opposed militarism, and disapproval of the estimates was one of the reasons he gave for resigning.

military-superiority.rationale: He refused to be party to the 1894 naval estimates meant to keep Britain's fleet ahead, judging the outlay a revolution in policy, and earlier called national 'prestige' the bane of upright politics.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: He campaigned over Bulgaria in 1876 for pressure on Turkey to end its abuses and, over Armenia in 1895-96, argued Britain had a right under the Cyprus Convention to act, though the form of armed action was left open.

open-diplomacy.rationale: He condemned a secret Anglo-Russian agreement made without the knowledge of Parliament as contrary to the principle of acting in concert.

avoid-permanent-military-alliances.rationale: His fourth principle of foreign policy was to avoid needless and entangling engagements, which add to commitments without adding strength.

nation-first.rationale: His third principle was to maintain the Concert of Europe, since common action neutralises each Power's selfish aims.

decide-locally.rationale: He argued in 1888 that Ireland should get everything in local self-government consistent with the unity of the Empire.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: In 'Kin Beyond Sea' he calls constitutional kingship a great political discovery and a beneficent institution that other European states may come to adopt.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: He describes the Sovereign as the symbol of the nation's unity and the apex of the social structure, acting only through ministers who bear the responsibility.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is about a constitutional or ceremonial crown, and the statement now asks only about passing real governing power to a child.

reviewHistory.rationale: He accepts the general rule of hereditary succession to the Crown as part of the constitution he praises, while noting it has no provision for a failed monarch.
reviewHistory.author: claude-sonnet-5-5

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: He notes that since 1688 the Crown's legal right has rested on contract and that breach of the contract destroys the title to subjects' allegiance.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: He calls the confinement of the power of the purse to the popular chamber the great conservator of liberty in all former times and regrets its weakening.

mixed-constitution.rationale: He praises the British constitution as a composite harmony of Crown, Lords and Commons, though he warns it works only if each party respects the others.

parliament-supreme.rationale: He holds that Ministers answerable to the Commons, not a separate royal sphere, decide in the last resort, and describes the omnipotence of Parliament and the ultimate superiority of force in the representative chamber.

second-chamber.rationale: His Government of Ireland Bill of 1886 gave the Irish legislature two orders sitting together, with a temporary veto for either, as a safeguard for deliberation.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: He presented Home Rule as leaving the absolute supremacy of the Imperial Parliament intact, saying the unity of the Empire rests on it.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: His 1886 bill provided safeguards for the Irish minority, including the two-order legislature, because of Ireland's divided history.

widespread-small-property.rationale: His 1886 Sale and Purchase of Land Bill aimed at turning Irish tenants into owners, with the state providing the funds, though the 1881 Act had instead fixed rents.

public-ownership.rationale: As President of the Board of Trade in 1844 he planned the ultimate acquisition of the railways by the public and said he was aware of the advantage of taking the telegraphs into government hands.

territorial-expansion.rationale: He called gratuitous annexations a political debauch, yet his government bombarded Alexandria and occupied Egypt in 1882, so his record points both ways.

office-by-exam.rationale: He championed competition in the civil service from the Crimean war and in 1870 devised the arrangement that opened government departments to open competitive examination.

women-suffrage.rationale: In his 1892 letter he earnestly hoped the Commons would decline to give a second reading to the Women's Suffrage Bill, objecting that it was a profound change to women's social function.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: He argued that men and women have unchangeable differences of type and social office set by their Maker, and so would not extend the full public franchise to women.

traditional-family.rationale: He feared that women's entry into public life would intrude on the family, which he called more fundamental and more sacred than the State.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: His 1851 letters to Lord Aberdeen denounced the Neapolitan government for contempt of law and justice in its prosecutions of political prisoners, a rule he called the negation of God erected into a system.

consent-of-governed.rationale: His 1870 cabinet memorandum urged that the wishes of the population be consulted before territory is transferred, a principle he treated as of general European concern.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: His government carried the 1881 Irish coercion measure suspending habeas corpus against agrarian conspiracy, though he accepted it reluctantly and doubted its efficacy.

regulate-corporations.rationale: As President of the Board of Trade he brought in the 1844 bill for the regulation of companies.
